title: Metzora: empty the house first (Leviticus 14:33–36)
hook: even walls can be afflicted; the house is emptied first to spare the owner's things

segments.voice: Yesterday in Metzora, a living bird flew free over an open field. Your line was let the bird go. Today, the affliction moves into the walls.

Black mold behind the bathroom tiles is its own kind of bad news. Something is wrong with the house itself, the place that was supposed to be safe. Leviticus 14 imagines something like it. A homeowner notices greenish or reddish streaks sunk into the stone, goes to the priest, and says, carefully, something like a plague has appeared in my house. Before the priest even steps through the door, the Torah gives an instruction that has nothing to do with stone at all.
screen: `MOLD BEHIND THE TILES.` → `STREAKS IN THE STONE.` → `BEFORE THE PRIEST GOES IN.`

segments.voice: The priest commands that the house be emptied before he goes in to look. Why? Once he declares the house unclean, everything still inside becomes unclean with it. The Mishnah asks what would be lost. Clothes and wood can be washed or purified, but earthenware pots can't; they'd have to be broken. And it draws a principle: the Torah has concern for people's property. Before it rules on the walls, it saves the dishes. Rashi adds a surprise, passing on an old midrash about why the walls were struck at all. The Amorites, it says, hid their gold in the walls of their houses during the forty years Israel was in the desert. A plague on the wall meant the stones came out, and the owner found treasure. An affliction that turns out to be a gift. It's a midrash, not something the verse says. And an honest note: a rabbinic opinion in the Talmud says a plagued house never actually happened and never will; it was written to be studied. Other rabbis answered that they knew of places where it had. The sources leave the disagreement standing. Whichever view you take, the verse keeps its order: empty it first. Take care of what matters before the verdict, because the verdict, whatever it is, shouldn't destroy more than it has to.
screen: `EMPTY THE HOUSE BEFORE HE LOOKS.` · `SAVE THE CLAY POTS.` · `THE GOLD IN THE WALLS.` · `NEVER HAPPENED, OR DID IT?` · then, large: `EMPTY IT FIRST.`

segments.voice: Picture one corner of your home that's been quietly building up: a drawer, a closet shelf, the chair that collects clothes. In your mind, empty it item by item onto the floor. Notice what you want to save, and what you've kept only because you never looked.
Metzora. The portion where even a house can be afflicted, and the priest has it emptied first, to spare the owner's things.
Your line: empty it first. Even a hard ruling can spare the dishes. That's day four hundred three.

howItsDone: The laws of afflicted houses are studied in the Mishnah's tractate Negaim and in the weekly reading of Metzora; the principle that the Torah has concern for people's property is cited in later Jewish law.

chat.says: Why did the priest have the house emptied before he even looked at the walls?
options: So the things inside wouldn't turn unclean; the Torah cares for people's property.
So he could search the empty rooms for the hidden Amorite gold first.
So nobody could hide the streaks behind furniture and fool him.
chat.meaning: Once the house is declared unclean, everything inside is too. The Mishnah says clay pots would have to be broken, so the Torah shows concern for property.

Mishnah.meaning: the early rabbis' collection of Jewish law and teaching

Rashi.meaning: the great medieval commentator on the Torah and Talmud

midrash.meaning: a rabbinic story or teaching that reads between the lines

Amorites.meaning: a people of the land, in Rashi's midrash

Talmud.meaning: the rabbis' great record of law and debate

notes: Lev 14:37 describes the streaks as greenish or reddish (yerakrakot or adamdamot); confirm wording.
Mishnah Negaim 12:5 (the Torah has concern for Israel's property; earthenware cannot be purified) cited from memory; confirm.
Rashi 14:34, from Vayikra Rabbah 17:6: Amorites hid treasure in walls during the 40 years in the desert. Confirm.
Sanhedrin 71a: 'a leprous house never was and never will be'; Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Tzadok cite places where one stood. Confirm names before they're named.
